subject: Density estimate lower than number of positively identified individuals!

messages.author: 9f147340cc598da4
messages.subject: Density estimate lower than number of positively identified individuals!
parts:
Dear SECR experts

I have computed an analysis in SECR on a small leopard dataset assuming a closed population, with an array of 68 cameras that were operating for 3 months and spaced at 2-3km intervals across a broadly homogenous habitat. Using secr.fit and the fit.buffer command as well as running esa plots for different buffer widths to estimate the appropriate buffer size, I fitted and compared three models according to time and/or behavioural variation. There were g0~t, g0~b and g0~b + t and all were similar in terms of fit. The best fit (g0~t) gave a density was 8.53 +/- 2.45, making the highest number of leopards 11 in the area of interest. This is all fine, but the number of independent individuals inputted was 13!

I assume that my model is flawed, as the estimated number should always be equal to or higher than the known number, right? Even if I misidentified the individuals, the model still "thinks" there are 13 individuals in the area so the model cannot be adequate?

I just wanted to check, as I can't work out what's gone wrong.

Many thanks
Bryony

messages.author: ec6a8aa7c56fe7fd
messages.subject: Re: Density estimate lower than number of positively identified individuals!
parts:
Hi Bryony,

It might be one of these things:

1) the difference between expected and realised abundance. There is more info in the help on region.N but in essence the first is an expectation over many hypothetical animal populations (multiple realisations of the process that SCR assumes generates animal activity centres). There's no need for this to be larger than the number of animals that you detected, or were there, at the time of your survey. The second is an estimate of how many leopards there were at the time of the survey, and will always be bigger than the number of animals you detected. 

2) with only 13 individuals fitting t and b models might be asking too much of the data, depending on numbers of recaptures. Maybe start with a null model and see if the pattern persists.

3) something went wrong in the conversion from density to abundance if you did this manually. You said density (number of animals per ha or km2) = 8.53 but treat it as an abundance (number of animals) in the comparison to 13. I guess you meant abundance all the way through though, but just putting here in case!

Hope that helps figure things out!

Ian

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Density estimate lower than number of positively identified individuals!
parts: Ah! A chance for me to warn against interpreting the 'effective trapping area' as a geographic area. It isn't. Effective trapping area is a number calculated as an amalgam of detection parameters (e.g., g0, sigma), the distribution of detectors, and the duration of sampling. Technical details in Borchers & Efford 2008. This clashes with informal pre-SECR concepts of effective trapping area (e.g. Otis et al. 1978).

parts:
Hi All

Thanks so much for your input. Tess - I took the fitted (real) density (D in below table) for the best model from AIC comparisons, which turned out to be the null (g0~1) and extrapolated it to my area of interest assuming that D within the ESA is the same as for the area of interest.so my density was 0.00017 leopards per ha and the AOI is 510000ha so I calculated the abundance of leopards to be 0.00017 x 51000 = 8.67.

Fitted (real) parameters evaluated at base levels of covariates
       link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
D       log 1.671791e-04 4.811537e-05 9.617398e-05 2.906074e-04
g0    logit 9.757486e-02 3.080448e-02 5.165495e-02 1.767099e-01
sigma   log 2.454027e+03 2.115681e+02 2.073150e+03 2.904878e+03

I did what Ian suggested i.e. running a simpler model - the null and low an behold it was by far the best model. But, as above it still yielded an estimate that was too low for the number of detections.

Bryony
